clinicalPearls: A rare congenital marrow-failure disorder combining amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia with proximal radioulnar synostosis (bony fusion limiting forearm rotation)
Caused by mutations in MECOM (EVI1) in most cases, or in HOXA11 in some families
Presents in infancy with thrombocytopenia and bleeding, often with limited pronation and supination of the forearm
The bone marrow characteristically shows reduced or absent megakaryocytes
There is a tendency for the cytopenia to progress to broader bone-marrow failure (aplastic anaemia) over time
Additional features can include clinodactyly, sensorineural hearing loss, and cardiac or renal anomalies
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation is the definitive treatment for evolving marrow failure
Diagnosis integrates the skeletal anomaly, marrow findings, and genetic testing of MECOM and HOXA11
reference.pathophysiology: MECOM (EVI1) and HOXA11 encode transcriptional regulators critical for haematopoietic stem-cell maintenance and megakaryocyte development, and MECOM also has roles in limb patterning. Pathogenic mutations impair the transcriptional programme that sustains stem-cell self-renewal and megakaryopoiesis, producing amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia that may extend to trilineage marrow failure. The overlapping developmental role in the upper limb explains the associated proximal radioulnar synostosis, linking the haematological and skeletal manifestations to disruption of shared regulatory pathways.
additionalDifferentials: Fanconi anaemia and other inherited bone-marrow failure syndromes
Diamond-Blackfan anaemia (when broader cytopenias are considered)
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and film documenting thrombocytopenia and any additional cytopenias
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine showing reduced or absent megakaryocytes
Forearm and elbow radiographs to demonstrate proximal radioulnar synostosis
Genetic testing of MECOM and HOXA11
Audiological, cardiac, and renal assessment for associated anomalies
Cytogenetics and marrow surveillance for evolving failure or clonal change
redFlags: Progression from isolated thrombocytopenia to pancytopenia indicating evolving marrow failure
Emergence of clonal cytogenetic abnormalities or dysplasia
Signs of an associated anomaly such as significant cardiac or renal dysfunction
reference.prognosis: Outlook is determined by progression to marrow failure; with vigilant monitoring and timely allogeneic stem-cell transplantation, outcomes can be good, whereas untreated evolving aplasia carries substantial risk.
pitfalls: Attributing the thrombocytopenia to immune causes and overlooking the skeletal clue of limited forearm rotation
Failing to anticipate and monitor for progression to full marrow failure
Not screening for associated cardiac, renal, and hearing abnormalities
Missing the diagnosis when radioulnar synostosis is subtle or not actively sought
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood
